title: A classical trajectory method for diatom-atom-atom ternary association reactions
summary: We introduce a classical trajectory method for calculating direct diatom-atom-atom ternary association re- action rates that incorporates the rotational degrees of freedom of the diatomic reactant. By treating the diatomic molecule as a rigid rotor, we include the effects of the anisotropy of the molecule-atom interaction and the dynamical effects of the rotational motion. We apply this approach to a system of experimental interest, CD+ + He + He, along with the isotopic variant CH+ + He + He -> CHHe+ + He, and examine the role of the internal, rotational degrees of freedom of the diatomic molecule. In particular, we find that in the regime where the collision energy is much smaller than the rotational energy of the entrance channel, the rotational motion leads to deviation from the classical threshold law by violating the assumptions of long-range capture theory models.

title: A Compact Single-Beam Optically Pumped Magnetometer Based on Absorption Detection
summary: We demonstrate a compact single-beam optically pumped magnetometer (OPM) employing a pure 87Rb microfabricated vapor cell with 500 Torr buffer gas. The residual magnetic field is actively minimized to below 400 pT through a combination of mu-metal magnetic shielding and internal compensation coils. We systematically characterize the OPM response as a function of laser detuning and optical intensity, and derive the magnetic-field sensitivity from the signal slope and noise amplitude spectral density. A best sensitivity of 11 fT/Hz^1/2 is achieved near the resonance transition at an optimal optical intensity, using a small cell volume of only 0.027 cm^3. Furthermore, a miniaturized OPM prototype was developed using a folded flexible printed circuit board (FPCB) to integrate the vapor cell, a compact heater, and magnetic-field coils into a cubic sensing head. Two coil configurations patterned directly on the FPCB were investigated. Under optimized operating conditions, the OPM prototype achieved a sensitivity of 66 fT/Hz^1/2. These results demonstrate that high-buffer-pressure single-beam OPMs can achieve excellent sensitivity, establishing a pathway toward compact and scalable arrays.

title: Single-step SU(3) Hahn Echo in a Qutrit Atom Interferometer
summary: The Hahn echo is a well-known dynamical decoupling method that refocuses the dephasing due to energy inhomogeneities of a spin-1/2 ensemble and is widely used to extend phase coherence in quantum computers and sensors. Extensions of such techniques beyond the spin-1/2 have been reported, but have mainly used SU(2) gates, limiting their scalability. Here, we generalize the Hahn echo to qutrits using single-step SU(3) gates and extend the coherence time by more than an order of magnitude. The gates are generated through optimal control theory and implemented in an ultracold atomic ensemble in free fall. A quantum process tomography procedure benchmarks the gates and yields fidelities of ~ 93%, limited mainly by state preparation and measurement errors. Due to the geometry of the laser beams, the generalized Hahn echo also realizes a three-path Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometer with two independent interferometric phase differences. Our results therefore establish SU(3) control for dynamical decoupling of qutrits and multi-path atom interferometers, with the latter opening the possibility for vector force measurements and interferometric tests of the validity of Born's rule.

title: Photoelectrons resolve the phase-dependent variance of bright squeezed vacuum
summary: The variance of bright squeezed vacuum (BSV) is not only strong but also phase dependent, yet recent strong-field experiments with BSV have recorded only its magnitude. A coherent field of the same color provides the phase reference that resolves this phase-dependent noise. Strong-field ionization of xenon by this light shows that the photoelectron yield follows the BSV quadrature along the coherent field, and that the nonlinearity of ionization amplifies the quadrature noise many times over in the electron yield. The noise is moreover distributed unevenly over the photoelectron momentum distribution, differing by an order of magnitude between ionization channels. Strong-field ionization thus offers a phase-sensitive, channel-resolved detector of quantum light, while the quadrature noise of quantum light offers a probe of the intensity dependence of individual ionization pathways.

title: Zero photoemission from icosahedral superatoms
summary: Photoemission is expected to occur when the photon energy exceeds the binding energy of an electron, with the photoemission yield generally remaining non-zero above this threshold. Yet, it can be suppressed at specific photon energies, a phenomenon known as the Cooper minimum. Although complete suppression represents an extreme limit of this phenomenon, such zero photoemission has previously been reported only for atoms with an outermost s-type orbital and has never been observed in non-atomic systems. Here, we demonstrate the deliberate realization of zero photoemission from Ag12W-, an artificial icosahedral superatom, by observing a vanishing photoemission cross section 0.85 eV above the detachment threshold and reproducing this behavior in theoretical simulations. These simulations predict that zero photoemission can be common in nearly spherical nanoclusters, a prediction we experimentally confirm using Ag12Mo-, an isoelectronic counterpart of Ag12W-. Because superatoms offer systematic control over both size and elemental composition using the periodic table, our findings establish a route toward active control of photoemission in finite-size quantum systems and stimulate further investigations of underexplored physical phenomena such as nondipole effects.

title: Thermal-noise-limited stabilization of a self-injection-locked diode laser using a miniature Fabry-Perot cavity
summary: We present an ultrastable laser system based on miniature core components: a self-injection-locked laser comprising a distributed-feedback laser diode and an integrated microring resonator, together with a 3-ml vacuum-gap Fabry-Perot cavity. By carefully addressing technical noise sources, in particular residual amplitude modulation, we demonstrate a thermal-noise-limited fractional frequency instability of $5\cdot10^{-15}$ for averaging times between 1 and 10 s, which is among the lowest reported for compact cavity-stabilized lasers. This performance is achieved with conventional multilayer mirrors and a moderate cavity finesse of $10^5$. Such stability of the output frequency, combined with the small size of the core components and a possibility to generate a Kerr frequency comb in the very same microring resonator, provides a path towards fully integrated photonic frequency references for transportable optical clocks and low-noise microwave synthesis.

title: CoPiT: A conditional Position-induced Transformer for aerodynamic field prediction on unstructured meshes
summary: High-fidelity Reynolds-averaged Navier--Stokes (RANS) simulations remain a standard tool for aerodynamic analysis, yet each solve on an unstructured mesh is computationally expensive, making many-query tasks such as design exploration, optimization, and multi-condition evaluation costly. Neural operators provide mesh-flexible surrogates for mapping geometry and operating conditions to flow fields; however, in many existing architectures, global parameters such as the freestream state and design variables are concatenated with pointwise inputs, leaving their influence on intermediate features implicit. This paper proposes CoPiT, a \textbf{Co}nditional \textbf{P}osition-induced \textbf{T}ransformer that builds on the Position-induced Transformer (PiT) as its geometric backbone and injects a global condition vector through multi-stage feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM), thereby making parametric modulation explicit while preserving geometry-based attention weights. The model is evaluated on two-dimensional AirfRANS airfoil fields, including scarce-data and extrapolation regimes, and on three-dimensional BlendedNet++ blended-wing-body surfaces. On the AirfRANS full-data test set, CoPiT reduces surface and volume losses by approximately 54\% and 24\% relative to Transolver, respectively, and achieves the lowest overall normalized test MSE among the compared baselines on BlendedNet++. Matched ablations show that FiLM conditioning generally improves upon input concatenation, while the preferred placement is task-dependent. CoPiT thus provides a practical operator-learning surrogate for parametric aerodynamics on unstructured meshes.

title: Coherent axion electrodynamics in OSIRIS: a counter-propagating axion-photon parametric instability
summary: We present a coherent axion-electrodynamics extension of the OSIRIS particle-in-cell code and use it to identify and benchmark a parametric axion-photon instability supported by two equal counter-propagating electromagnetic pumps. The module evolves a cell-centered axion field together with a separately stored first-order electromagnetic response on the native staggered OSIRIS grid. Re-examining the previously proposed strictly co-linear branch shows that it is removed when the axion-Maxwell equations are reduced consistently. A closely related standing-wave geometry, however, supports a distinct Floquet instability. We derive the coupled Floquet problem for an equal-amplitude counter-propagating pump pair and obtain a reduced analytic growth rate and cutoff for the dominant long-wavelength envelope branch. For an axion mass-to-pump-frequency ratio of 0.06 and a per-beam vector-potential amplitude of 0.3, simulations at coupling strengths of 0.60, 0.80, and 1.00 reproduce both the growth-rate spectrum and the coupling-dependent instability boundary. The reduced theory predicts envelope-mode cutoffs of 8.44, 10.80, and 13.23, while OSIRIS finds exponential growth through modes 8, 10, and 13, respectively, with the next resolved modes stable. The electromagnetic diagnostics additionally resolve exponentially growing sidebands at twice the pump wavenumber, while the zero-wavenumber electric component exhibits no sustained growth, as expected for the unstable Floquet eigenvector. The agreement provides an end-to-end benchmark of the coherent axion-electromagnetic coupling and demonstrates that parametric growth of the axion field is present in a two-beam pump geometry.

title: Anchored HLLD: A Riemann solver for a hypoelastic diffuse-interface model of compressible fluid-solid interaction
summary: We present an HLLD Riemann solver for a multicomponent hypoelastic diffuse-interface model of compressible fluid-solid interaction, with no separately computed interface and a deviatoric stress advanced by an objective hypoelastic rate law outside conservation-law form. The difficulty specific to this model is that the stress evolution is nonconservative and, unlike the familiar volume-fraction terms of Kapila-type models, cannot be left outside the Riemann solve once the shear waves are resolved. The shear coefficient $ρ(G+τ_{xx})$ sets the impedance of the resolved shear waves and so belongs to their eigenstructure. Anchored HLLD carries it inside the solve by evaluating the HLLD fan twice at each face, anchored in turn to each adjacent cell-centered state, with every cell advancing from the flux anchored to its own state. HLL, HLLC, and anchored HLLD form a three-tier hierarchy of increasing wave resolution in one framework. We prove local structural properties: consistency at the reconstruction order, exact species-mass conservation, and tangential-momentum and energy drift vanishing under refinement at the reconstruction's face-jump order on smooth fields, with one-dimensional tests illustrating these structural properties and demonstrating first-order drift convergence on discontinuous fields. Across one-dimensional tests and two-dimensional production simulations in the open-source solver MFC, anchored HLLD resolves both the material contact and the shear waves, HLLC the contact alone, and HLL neither sharply. Where refinement studies are shown, anchored HLLD converges toward exact or semi-analytic solutions. A three-dimensional shock-ellipsoid interaction demonstrates the solver with all six stress components active.

title: QuantumBilliards.jl: An extensible, user friendly, high-performance Julia library for the large scale computation of spectra and eigenstates of quantum billiards and related problems
summary:
We present QuantumBilliards.jl, an open-source Julia library providing a suite of numerical solvers for the two-dimensional interior Helmholtz eigenproblem with Dirichlet boundary conditions, a paradigmatic model in quantum chaos. The library implements conventional wavenumber-sweep techniques together with several accelerated eigensolvers: the Vergini--Saraceno scaling method, the expanded boundary integral method (EBIM), Beyn's contour-integral method, and the Compact Rational Krylov (CORK) method. It provides a common framework for constructing billiard geometries, exploiting discrete symmetries, computing eigenvalues and eigenstates, and treating smooth, cornered, and multiply connected domains. The library further includes reconstruction of eigenfunctions from boundary normal derivatives and the computation of Poincaré--Husimi (PH) phase-space representations.
  Available at: https://github.com/Quantum-Chaos-Julia/QuantumBilliards.jl.

title: Sensitivity-Guided Parameter Estimation of Bubbly Liquid via a Nonlinear Wave Equation and Physics-InformedNeuralNetworks
summary: Interactions between ultrasound and microbubbles underlie a range of biomedical and industrial applications, yet predicting how the physical parameters of the medium and bubbles govern nonlinear wave propagation remains difficult. This study proposes a parameter estimation framework that combines a Korteweg-de Vries-Burgers (KdVB) equation, describing weakly nonlinear wave propagation in a bubbly liquid, with a physics-informed neural network (PINN). The contributions are threefold. First, the PINN reproduces the reference solution of the governing equation in the forward problem, with a near-zero prediction error at the initial time that confirms the initial condition is enforced exactly as intended. Second, prior to inverse estimation, a sensitivity analysis is introduced that quantifies, at both the coefficient and solution levels, how each of eight physical parameters influences the KdVB equation, allowing the expected difficulty of estimating each parameter to be assessed in advance. Third, based on this assessment, single-parameter inverse estimation is performed for seven of the eight parameters using the PINN. Liquid viscosity, bubble initial radius, liquid density, sound speed, and liquid pressure are estimated with errors of 0.8-2.1%, the polytropic exponent converges only partially, and the surface tension coefficient cannot be estimated at all, consistent with the sensitivity analysis. These results establish a general framework for identifying and estimating the physical parameters governing nonlinear wave propagation in bubbly liquids from observed waveform data.

title: Compression of turbulent flow data through an extended space-time correlation: certification against the modal energy budget
comment: 14 pages, 12 figures, 4 tables. Submitted to Computers & Fluids
summary: The fidelity of direct numerical simulation now outpaces the storage and data-movement capacity available for the resulting fields. We present an open, distributed, GPU-accelerated low-rank compression framework for large turbulent flow databases. We assess it using two direct numerical simulations of a controlled diffusion compressor cascade under laminar and turbulent inflow conditions. Compression is formulated using a correlation operator over space and time, which is two orders of magnitude larger than that of snapshot POD. Its dominant range is extracted with a randomized range finder based on communication-avoiding hierarchical QR. The compressed databases are evaluated through a hierarchy of increasingly strict diagnostics, from instantaneous reconstruction and second-order statistics to the modal turbulent kinetic energy budget and its nonlinear interscale transfer. The budget terms are far more sensitive to compression than fieldwise or one-point errors. They remain accurate at conservative compression and degrade sharply once the retained energy is relaxed. The near-wall dissipation and the interscale transfer degrade the most and set the admissible compression level. An aggressive reduction preserves every one-point statistic to within a few per cent while corrupting both by an order of magnitude more. The dissipation error is confined to the viscous sublayer and grows with the development of the boundary layer. It is carried by the high-order modes. For both inflows, the linear budget terms scale with the discarded energy to the power $0.8$ and the triadic transfer to a power above one.

title: Let's Do Turbulence Right: In Space and Time!
summary: The three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations govern fluid turbulence, a chaotic and non-linear physical phenomenon characterized by complex eddies interacting across vast spatial and temporal scales. A numerically accurate modeling of this multi-scale energy cascade requires fully resolving both the fine spatial structures and the continuous temporal evolution of the flow field. In this paper, we leverage massive, time-resolved direct numerical simulations, which exceed 28 TB per run, to assess how numerical choices govern the resolved (3+1)-dimensional physics of turbulent flows. Building on this analysis, we study how neural networks represent the recorded turbulent motion. Our results highlight that spatial and temporal assessments can disagree for both numerical records and learned representations. We therefore call on the machine learning community to treat (3+1)-dimensional turbulence as a four-dimensional phenomenon.

title: Solving and Learning Navier-Stokes Dynamics with the Neural Basis Method
summary: Physics-informed machine learning has become a major direction in predictive modeling of fluid dynamics, combining governing physics with learned representations. Yet prevailing formulations neither guarantee that small PDE-residual losses imply small solution errors nor scale effectively with increasing problem size. Here we present the neural basis method (NBM) as a new approach for Navier--Stokes dynamics. NBM is built on a ``representation-then-projection'' principle: fixed neural bases define the representation space, while projection of the governing equations determines the expansion coefficients. The same bases define common coordinates for the parametric solution manifold, recasting operator learning as a parameter-to-coefficient mapping and enabling scalability by removing explicit spatial dependence. For incompressible flow, NBM yields a velocity-only formulation whose residual provides an a posteriori velocity-error estimate, establishing a certified, data-free training objective for coefficient learning. Theoretical analysis and numerical experiments demonstrate the accuracy, efficiency, generalization, and scalability of NBM, with substantial improvements over baselines.

title: Heat vortices and the vorticity triplet in kinetic phonon transport: a fluid-dynamical perspective
summary: From a novel fluid-dynamical perspective, the present study investigates the heat-current vortices and heat vorticity in heat conduction process of solid materials. The heat vorticity $\bmω$, defined as the curl of the heat-flux field, is decomposed into the orbital-rotation $\bm{R}$ and spin $\bm{S}$, which collectively constitute the heat-vorticity triplet $(\bm{R},\bm{S},\bmω)$, extending beyond the existing single-vorticity research paradigm. As an illustrative example, kinetic phonon transport in a 2D porous solid structure is examined based on the numerical solutions of the Peierls-Boltzmann equation under the Callway dual-relaxation-time approximation. The physical characteristics of heat vortices and the vorticity triplet patterns are analyzed across different kinetic regimes in the phase diagram of the normal (N) and resistive (R) scattering processes.... In the hydrodynamic limit, the boundary generation mechanism of heat vorticity is further elucidated based on the Guyer-Krumhansl (G-K) equation generated from the truncated Chapman-Enskog (C-E) expansion. The boundary heat vorticity flux (BHVF) is proposed as a new concept for describing the local rate at which heat vorticity is generated at the boundary of a solid material. The general expression for the BHVF is rigorously derived for phonon hydrodynamics, and for the 2D steady hydrodynamic phonon transport case, we find that the BHVF is solely attributed to the tangential component of the net heat flux deviating from the classical Fourier heat flux. Furthermore, we show that the total vorticity contained in a control volume arises from the spatiotemporal accumulation of the BHVF, weighted by the memory kernel arising from the R scattering. The proposed theory and findings herein could be valuable for understanding the diverse vortical-flow phenomena in condensed matter systems.

title: IMRFit: Interactive Simulation and Constitutive-Model Fitting for Inertial Microcavitation Rheometry
summary:
Inertial microcavitation rheometry (IMR) characterizes the high-rate mechanical response of soft materials from the rapid expansion and collapse of a microscopic bubble. In a typical IMR experiment, high-speed imaging provides the bubble radius as a function of time, R(t), and material parameters are identified by comparing the measured response with simulations that couple bubble dynamics to a constitutive description of the surrounding medium. This inverse analysis requires repeated forward simulations and careful control of experimental inputs, material parameters, and fitting settings.
  IMRFit is an open-source Python desktop application that brings these steps into an interactive environment for forward simulation, parameter identification, and constitutive-model comparison. Users can import experimental radius-time data, select a bubble-dynamics formulation and constitutive model, inspect simulated responses, fit material parameters, and organize batch fitting and parameter-sweep jobs. IMRFit includes Neo-Hookean Kelvin-Voigt and generalized Maxwell-Ogden-based models, among other constitutive options, and supports additional models through JSON descriptors and Python solver entry points. It also integrates fitting-window selection, visualization, and data export into a single workflow.

title: Physics-informed neural network (PINN) approximations of capillary menisci in polygonal channels
comment: 17 pages, 5 figures. Includes the main text and complete Supplementary Material
summary: In a zero-gravity cylindrical container, a meniscus can span a square or equilateral-triangular cross-section only at contact angles at or above the respective Concus-Finn critical angles of 45 degrees and 60 degrees. We study strong-form physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) across these thresholds under fixed collocation and optimization budgets. Classical capillary flux balance yields a lower bound on the combined interior and wall residual loss for arbitrary positive sampling densities. In the tested nonexistence regime, several degrees below the critical angles, independently evaluated network losses are 1.6-1.9 times this bound. A polynomial least-squares comparison supports the same geometric interpretation. The PINNs still return smooth graphs with finite axial extent, even though the prescribed equilibrium problem has no spanning graph solution. Their small interior residuals coexist with wall-flux deficits near corners, where adjoining contact-angle conditions demand more flux than a finite-slope graph can supply. Residuals vary on both sides of the critical angle, while the bound tends uniformly to zero at threshold for fixed wall weight. These results give a geometric scale for interpreting the computed loss and locate the incompatibility that a small interior residual can conceal.

title: Scaling the Wavelength to Optimize Ultrafast Laser Processing of Bandgap Materials
summary: The spectral characteristics of ultrashort laser pulses offer unique possibilities to control interactions in space and time as well as the subsequent material responses. In particular, selecting the wavelength predefines the fundamental mechanisms governing laser-matter interaction, and thus, how energy is deposited. This Chapter provides an overview on how the essential physical effects in ultrafast laser-matter interaction scale with the wavelength, and the consequences for bandgap material processing applications. First, we recall the main spectral properties of bandgap materials and discuss the important question of the expected processing resolutions depending on wavelength. Then, recent studies on the impact of the wavelength in ultrafast laser-dielectric interaction are presented. Finally, we present how the latest developments in infrared ultrafast laser sources can be advantageously utilized to internally process narrow-gap materials despite challenges related to increased nonlinearities.

title: CBTV: Colour Bean Tracking Velocimetry for Dense Granular Flows
summary: Conventional particle tracking velocimetry (PTV) has been the standard diagnostic tool for studying fluid and granular flows. However, in dense granular systems, the average distance moved by particles between frames can approach or exceed inter-particle spacing, demanding ultra-high frame rates. Furthermore, neighbouring particles may move together, and common velocity-based prediction fails after energetic collisions. Existing methods struggle to track granular particles without losing identities or swapping. We present Colour Bean Tracking Velocimetry (CBTV), a training-free multi-pass method leveraging multicoloured particles to achieve enhanced tracking. CBTV first matches constellations of neighbouring coloured particles as single units, guided by a cross-correlation motion prior, and only then assigns the remaining particles individually. We compare it with 12 baseline tracker configurations, from classical linkers to graph-neural-network and transformer models, on 59 cases from 15 simulated discrete-element granular flows with exact ground truth (0.006-9 diameters/frame). CBTV matches or exceeds every tracker tested on an impulsive collision at every displacement. Its advantage lies in dense flows in which particles move between about half and twice their spacing per frame, where links between frames are ambiguous. On agitated shear flow, a colour relaxation tracker, which also uses neighbour context, matches or narrowly exceeds CBTV. Where links are unambiguous, CBTV is close to the best tracker, and beyond about two to three particle diameters per frame, the range of its motion prior, trackers that compensate for bulk motion are more accurate. For experimentalists, dense granular flows of coloured particles can be tracked at displacements per frame where trackers without neighbour context lose identities, easing the demand for ultra-high frame rates without training data.

title: Polarization-encoded photon statistics for counting dipole emitters
summary: Counting the emitters within a diffraction-limited region is a prerequisite for localizing overlapping molecules. Under pulsed excitation, each molecule emits at most one photon per pulse, so photon-number-resolved detection can count emitters without resolving them. But the required number of pulses grows steeply with the emitter number. Here we show that polarization, conventionally used to measure the orientations of dipole emitters, also carries information on their number. Because mean polarization-resolved signals are unchanged when every emitter is replaced by multiple dimmer copies, this information resides in the photon statistics within each pulse, which polarization reshapes in two ways. Linearly polarized excitation at three angles increases the sub-Poissonian deficit of the photon count by a factor of 1.5 for any emitter orientation, and detection in four polarization channels reveals the emitter number through how the photons of multiphoton pulses are distributed among the channels. Maximum-likelihood simulations for two to five emitters of unknown orientations and brightnesses show that three-angle excitation reduces the required number of pulses by about 2.3-fold, close to the predicted $1.5^2=2.25$, and that adding four-channel detection raises the reduction to as much as 4.8-fold. These gains require only polarization optics added to photon-number-resolved detection.

title: High-order Simulation of Nearly Hydrostatic Atmospheric Flows
summary: Accurate simulation of atmospheric flows is challenging. Low-Mach-number dynamics often need to be resolved in the presence of a dominant, nearly hydrostatic background state. Conventional upwind numerical fluxes can introduce excessive acoustic-speed-based dissipation in the low-Mach regime. Discretization errors in the balance law can also generate spurious motion. This work investigates these two issues within a high-order Direct Flux Reconstruction (DFR) framework coupled with a third-order exponential time integrator for the 3D compressible Euler equations with gravity. Low-Mach-number accuracy is addressed using a modified AUSM$^+$-up flux, denoted AUSM$^+$-upH. Preservation of the background equilibrium is improved through a deviation-based formulation. The resulting approach is assessed using a hierarchy of idealized atmospheric test cases. The results show that AUSM$^+$-upH preserves low-Mach flow structures more effectively than the more dissipative Rusanov flux. However, reduced numerical dissipation also makes AUSM$^+$-upH more sensitive to residual errors in the discrete hydrostatic balance. The deviation formulation substantially suppresses these errors by several orders of magnitude, with the strongest improvement observed for flows over orography. Overall, AUSM$^+$-upH exhibits greater robustness when combined with the deviation formulation across the atmospheric test cases considered.

title: Video-rate quantitative phase and polarimetric imaging (QP2I) for label-free imaging of contracting muscle cells
summary: Quantitative phase imaging (QPI) has become a standard approach for label-free microscopy of transparent specimens, mapping the optical path length. However, the isotropic phase is blind to the molecular order underlying optical anisotropy. Implementations that also add quantitative contrast to birefringence, rely on multi-frame illumination or polarization-state scanning, or on dedicated interferometric hardware, that trade away acquisition speed or the simplicity of a standard microscope. We present Quantitative Phase and Polarimetric Imaging (QP2I), a computational imaging framework that converts a standard differential interference contrast (DIC) microscope with a polarization camera into a single-shot, video-rate, dual-contrast imaging system. We developed a new globally regularized phase reconstruction that eliminates artifacts of prior DIC-to-QPI approaches, providing quantitative phase information and used per-pixel Stokes-based reconstruction to obtain quantitative anisotropic retardance. We validate the approach across simulations, static reference targets, fixed muscle tissue and living dynamically moving cells. Thereby, QP2I enables to study contractile dynamics in live cardiomyocytes all-optically and label-free. It provides both structural and functional readouts at frame rates that are sufficient to temporally resolve fast cardiomyocyte contractions. While conventional fluorescent labels bleach out over time, perturb physiology, and preclude long-term monitoring, QP2I provides similar established structural readouts, such as frame-by-frame sarcomere length, as well as previously inaccessible measurements, like quantitative analysis of retardance changes during muscle contraction, as a direct optical signature of muscle photoelasticity. QP2I thus enables long-term, label-free interrogation of dynamic cellular processes at quantitative contrast.

title: Tokamak-SI: Interpreting Tokamak Discharges with Labeled Catalogs
summary: Finding which phenomena occur in a tokamak discharge, and when, is often a manual task. Previous efforts at labeling events have been task-specific, each with its own corpus of data. We introduce Tokamak-SI, which combines the labels and labeling methods of many earlier studies into a single scalable, time-aligned, and categorical dataset covering observations from confinement, detachment, alfven eigenmodes (AE), edge localized modes (ELM), sawtooth, tearing modes (TM), and resistive wall modes in DIII-D tokamak. Models based on this, which can extend the labels to new shots, match or beat earlier detectors on its labels, including for AE, ELM, and TM detection. Tokamak-SI is intended to enable task-specific benchmarking, physics-searchable archives, and direct identification of key events during an experiment.

title: Ideal interaction dynamics of defects and background fields in condensed matter
summary: While defect dynamics in condensed matter systems is widely studied and several methods are available to track the defect position over time, the formulation of dynamical models for the coupled evolution of both defect and background field quantities seems to be more challenging. Yet, the overall behavior of a system containing moving defects is strongly influenced by this defect-field interaction. Here, we propose a modeling framework for the conservative coupled evolution of the defect density and the background fields upon focusing on two relevant cases of study: the Gross-Pitaevskii theory of quantum fluids and the Ericksen-Leslie model of nematic liquid crystals. To achieve the coupled evolution, we combine the Euler-Poincaré variational setting of continuum dynamics with the gauge theory of topological defects. While the latter allows us to overcome certain ambiguities in definition of the defect density, the Euler-Poincaré method provides a unified modeling approach in the absence of defect reconnection.

title: Integrated elliptical III-V nanopillar arrays on silicon for dual photodetection and light emission
summary: Next-generation on-chip photonic devices require compact, energy-efficient components integrating photodetection and light emission on silicon platforms. Achieving broadband photodetection combined with efficient emission in a single nanoscale device remains challenging. Here, we demonstrate elliptical nanopillar arrays monolithically integrated as III-V-on-Si templates, exhibiting broadband photoresponse across visible to near-infrared wavelengths, dynamic neuron-like graded responses under modulated light, and pronounced electroluminescence at around 865 nm under forward bias. The nanostructured elliptical geometry approach enhances optical absorption and carrier dynamics within an active area significantly smaller than commercial detectors, enabling responsivities up to 0.55 A/W at 830 nm in compact nanoarrays. This work advances the development of miniaturized active nanophotonic devices suitable for integrated sensing, emitting and communication circuits, and neuromorphic processing on silicon substrates.

title: Predicting Negative Triangularity Edge Confinement with a Neutral-Coupled Full-f Gyrokinetic Model
summary: Global full-f gyrokinetic simulations coupled to a reduced neutral-fluid model reproduce key DIII-D experimental trends and identify mechanisms underlying improved confinement in negative triangularity (NT) configurations relative to positive triangularity (PT). Using Gkeyll, we simulate DIII-D inner-wall-limited discharges across the confined edge, scrape-off layer (SOL), and sheath boundaries, allowing the edge electric field to evolve self-consistently. Compared with an adaptive recycling-source model, the reduced neutral fluid model improves particle and energy balances and brings the simulated density and temperature profiles into closer agreement with measurements, with minimal additional computational cost. In NT, suppressed turbulent fluxes coincide with a broad, stationary zonal flow inside the last closed flux surface, whereas PT develops transient, fragmented shear layers. Spectral analysis indicates that modified fluctuation phase relationships and enhanced zonal shear both contribute to transport suppression despite broadly comparable fluctuation amplitudes. The larger co-current departure from a locally matched bi-Maxwellian in NT suggests a velocity-selective kinetic process that may help establish the edge radial electric field by modifying flows or current balance. These results identify kinetic and turbulent mechanisms associated with improved NT confinement within an experimentally established ELM-free regime and demonstrate the importance of coupling gyrokinetic plasma dynamics with neutral interactions across the confined plasma and SOL.

title: Physics Informed Neural Network for Multi-dimensional Turbulent Self-gravitating Flows
summary: Molecular clouds exhibit complex, multi-scale dynamics driven by the interplay of turbulence, self-gravity, and gas pressure. Modelling these systems with conventional grid-based methods becomes increasingly expensive as spatial resolution and dimensionality increase. Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) offer a mesh-free alternative by incorporating the governing equations directly into the training objective, but their ability to model realistic turbulent self-gravitating flows remains largely unexplored. We apply PINNs to isothermal molecular clouds initialized with astrophysically motivated turbulent velocity fields, considering subsonic and supersonic evolution in two and three dimensions. We benchmark the predicted density and velocity fields against the finite-volume code Athena++. PINNs accurately recover the global evolution of the flow over multiple free-fall times across turbulent realizations, Mach numbers, and dimensionalities. Their training cost also exhibits weak dependence on spatial resolution, increasing by less than 25% from 128^3 to 1024^3 in our experiments. These results demonstrate that PINNs can model substantially more realistic self-gravitating turbulent flows than previously explored and provide a promising complementary framework for studying these systems.

title: Supercontinuum-driven broadband Fourier-transform photothermal microspectroscopy
summary: Chemical characterization of microscopic samples often requires resolving multiple, widely separated vibrational absorption bands, including their positions and spectral shapes. Photothermal microspectroscopy provides a route to localized vibrational measurements by detecting absorption-induced thermal responses with a separate optical probe. However, rapid acquisition of broadband photothermal spectra remains challenging when spectral information is collected through sequential wavelength tuning. Here, we develop a supercontinuum (SC)-driven Fourier-transform photothermal (FT-PT) microspectroscopy platform that combines broadband near-infrared excitation with rapid-scan interferometric acquisition for localized vibrational measurements. In this approach, an interferometrically modulated SC pump induces wavelength-dependent photothermal responses in the sample, which are detected through a co-propagating visible probe beam and reconstructed by Fourier transformation. Using a 1.65-2.35 um spectral window, we demonstrate broadband photothermal spectra of aqueous samples with acquisition rates of approximately one spectrum per second. The system simultaneously resolves multiple molecular absorption features in a water-dimethyl sulfoxide mixture and reproduces the near-infrared absorption characteristics of liquid water with high spectral fidelity. Extending beyond homogeneous liquids, a dark-field detection configuration enables broadband photothermal spectroscopy of an individual 6 um polystyrene particle in an aqueous environment. This SC-based FT-PT microspectroscopy approach provides a rapid and broadband platform for localized vibrational characterization of liquid and microscopic samples, enabling chemical analysis with microscale spatial selectivity.

title: Plasma transport by carrier electrons: delocalization length for heat-flux
summary: The delocalization length $λ_d=λ_{ei} Z/\sqrt{Z+4.45}$ is an improved heat-flux non-locality metric accounting for the localizing effect of electron-electron collisions on the electron population carrying heat-flux. Magnetization also localizes the carrier electrons; the delocalization Hall parameter $ψ_d=13.5 χZ/(Z+4.62)$ shows that this occurs at a faster rate than magnetization of thermal conductivity ($ψ_κ= 9.94χ(Z+0.17)/(Z+5.88)$). The traditional Knudsen number, which uses the electron-ion mean-free path, does not fairly represent non-locality across ionization and magnetization; $Kn_d = 8.28λ_{d\bot}/L_T$ should instead be used. The kinetic understanding of the three magnetized heat-flux components is unified in the linear regime with a full electron-electron collision operator and a converged harmonic expansion of the electron distribution (up to $f_6$). Righi-Leduc heat-flux is found to delocalize easier than its perpendicular counterpart, due to its carriers being higher energy electrons. This approach lays the groundwork for a consistent treatment of the kinetically-modified induction equation.

title: Chaos Made Visible: Active particles trace Lorenz-like attractors in physical space
summary: Chaotic attractors are typically visualized in an abstract phase space. Here we show that an orientable active particle moving through a steady, two-dimensional, multivortex flow can trace a Lorenz-like chaotic attractor in its real space trajectory. Despite the flow being strictly time independent, coupling between particle position and orientation creates a three-dimensional nonlinear dynamical system. For suitable particle shape and swimming speed, the trajectory organizes into a striking two-lobed geometry reminiscent of the classical Lorenz attractor. A structured first return map, positive largest Lyapunov exponent, and a broadband power spectrum establish that the underlying motion is chaotic. Varying the swimming speed reveals a rich sequence of dynamical regimes as self-propulsion breaks streamline confinement and reorganizes the particle motion. Our results demonstrate how an internal orientational degree of freedom can make chaotic dynamics directly visible in physical space, allowing a single active particle to trace a chaotic attractor as it moves through an otherwise steady flow.

title: Computational imaging through turbid, bubbly and flowing water near the telescope
summary: Cameras in the surf zone or behind ship wakes look through turbid, bubbly, moving water close to the lens, yet restoration networks are usually scored only on displayed images. We introduce a measured dataset of a telescope viewing displayed images and physical objects through a 25~mm water layer 45~mm in front of its objective, under seven combinations of flow, bubbles and turbidity, with clear-water recordings as a second reference. Because the suspension scatters light far outside the 1.3\textdegree{} field of view, turbidity mainly removes contrast, 4.4- to 4.8-fold on a Siemens star. Restoring the mean of eight frames improves structural similarity (SSIM) by 0.032 over a single frame, and learned fusion of the frames adds little. One raw frame supports five-category recognition (96.8\%) as well as restored images. Adding synthetic training pairs leaves display-image scores unchanged but raises the correlation of a restored Siemens star with its clear-water recording from below 0.5 to above 0.9. These networks also improve ordinary underwater photographs without retraining, where training on measured pairs alone fails. Scoring against the digital source or a clear-water recording reverses the ranking of raw and restored images. These results support a simple pipeline: average the frames, classify raw frames directly, and restore with networks trained on measured and synthetic pairs.

title: Two-component Bayesian modeling in the data analysis of collective Thomson scattering
comment: 11 pages, 9 figures. Accepted for publication in Plasma and Fusion Research on October 16, 2026
summary: We apply Bayesian inference to the analysis of collective Thomson scattering (CTS) spectra, a diagnostic technique for determining local plasma parameters. Using the population annealing Monte Carlo (PAMC) method, we evaluate the posterior probability density functions (PDFs) for six plasma parameters. The analysis is performed separately for the ion acoustic wave (IAW) and electron plasma wave (EPW) features and jointly for both features. The results show that the combined analysis provides constraints on all six parameters, although the degree of constraint depends on the parameter, whereas the separate analyses provide strong constraints only on complementary subsets of the parameters. In particular, the combined analysis provides a clear constraint on the ion charge state, which is not determined by either separate analysis alone. These findings demonstrate the importance of Bayesian modeling that accounts for the two-component nature of plasmas, consisting of ions and electrons.

title: When does boundary-condition uncertainty outweigh thermal and vegetation effects in street canyon flow? A global sensitivity analysis of input uncertainty
summary: Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) is increasingly used to resolve wind, heat, and pollution patterns in cities with high fidelity but high computational cost. Thermal effects and vegetation are often neglected despite being important drivers, yet their influence may be masked by variability from other uncertain inputs. This work determines how precisely model parameters and boundary conditions must be known for these effects to govern output uncertainty in the velocity, temperature, and concentration fields of a two-dimensional street canyon. A global Sobol analysis of 24 parameters is made tractable by a surrogate trained on Reynolds-Averaged Navier--Stokes (RANS) simulations, combining principal component analysis (PCA) with multilayer perceptrons (MLPs). Two ventilation regimes assess the variance due to thermal and vegetation parameters as uncertainty in all other inputs is progressively reduced. At typical uncertainty levels, turbulence closure constants and inflow turbulence profiles govern variability in all three fields in both regimes. Under weak ventilation, solar forcing becomes the main source of temperature variability once the remaining uncertainties are halved, and of concentration variance once they are reduced to a quarter (about $\pm11\%$ for the dominant closure constant and $\pm12\%$ for the emission rate). In contrast, vegetation contributes significantly at typical uncertainty levels. Under strong ventilation, however, the canopy never overtakes the closure constants, even when the dominant one is known to $\pm5\%$. Spatially, both effects peak at road level and along canyon walls, which influence outdoor exposure and indoor infiltration, suggesting that high-resolution exposure studies should account for them.

title: Stochastic Analysis of Laser Phase Noise in Photonics-Assisted Radio Frequency Beamforming
summary: This paper develops a stochastic model for quantifying the impact of laser phase noise on photonics-assisted radio frequency (RF) beamforming. Unlike conventional deterministic models, the presented theoretical framework captures the statistical randomness associated with the RF array factor of beamforming networks driven by finite-linewidth lasers. Fourier-domain analysis reveals that laser phase noise reshapes the spatial coherence function of such beamforming networks, inducing coherent RF aperture shrinkage, beam-pattern distortion, and directivity degradation. The analysis highlights that beamforming network architectures employing nanosecond-scale optical differential delays can exhibit substantial performance degradation even when driven by commercially available narrow-linewidth (kHz-range) lasers. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that average RF power gain gets downscaled and fluctuations dominate in large-aperture beamforming networks due to phase noise, imposing an upper limit on the maximum achievable RF antenna array-size. The reported results highlight the quantitative performance and scalability limits imposed by laser phase noise in photonics-assisted RF beamforming, offering key design guidelines for implementing large-scale beamforming networks in next-generation wireless communications, sensing, radar, and radio astronomy applications.

title: Overview of Enhanced D-alpha and Quasi Continuous Exhaust H-modes at DIII-D
summary: We review the Enhanced D-alpha (EDA) and Quasi-continuous Exhaust (QCE) H-modes that have recently been achieved in the DIII-D tokamak. These scenarios are free of large type-I edge-localized modes (ELMs) and achieved at high fueling compatible with divertor detachment. This makes them promising operational regimes as ELMs are a major risk for fusion pilot plants (FPPs). Access to EDA H-mode and the associated quasi-coherent mode (QCM) was observed at low heating power barely above the L-H power threshold, and increased density enabled access to EDA H-mode even at higher heating powers. The QCE H-mode was achieved at simultaneously high density and heating power, characterized also by a QCM and small ELMs with transient peaks of the total power into the divertor below about 3MW, in line with observations at ASDEX Upgrade. During the QCE H-mode, the turbulence parameter alpha_t at the separatrix is about 1 and does not separate ELMy or EDA from QCE H-modes well. Peeling ballooning stability calculations suggest that the EDA H-mode pedestal is limited by transport far away from ideal magnetohydrodynamic instability, and the QCE H-mode pedestal operates close to the ballooning branch of the stability boundary. BOUT++ simulations qualitatively reproduce the pressure collapse characteristics of the different regimes and suggest an important role of n ~ 50 resistive ballooning modes localized near the separatrix at the X-point during EDA and QCE H-modes. This work provides a foundation and guidance for further research on the access conditions and physics mechanisms of EDA and QCE H-modes necessary for the extrapolation of these regimes towards an FPP.

title: Strongly non-linear continuous model for wave propagation in 2D granular media: derivation and hyperbolicity analysis
summary: In this work, we develop a nonlinear continuum model for wave propagation in two-dimensional granular materials, building on key ideas from Nesterenko's work. Starting from the Hertzian contact law and neglecting contact friction, we derive an effective continuum description through homogenization, assuming spherical, monodisperse grains, local periodicity, and the Cauchy--Born hypothesis. The resulting strain-gradient model depends on both the first and second gradients of the displacement field. We analyse the hyperbolicity of the leading-order system through its eigenvalues and eigenvectors, establishing conditions for hyperbolicity within a restricted deformation domain. The model is solved using an explicit finite-volume method to investigate gravitational settling and wave propagation. We derive analytical expressions for the longitudinal and transverse wave speeds and highlight their dependence on depth. Finally, the predictions of the continuum model are compared with existing discrete-element simulations. This formulation allows several extensions, including more complex packing geometries, contact laws, and large-deformation regimes in which the contact network can evolve.

title: From Hollow Waveguides to Mie Voids: Low-Index Light Confinement
summary: The confinement of light within optically thin media challenges the conventional view that optical localization requires high-index dielectric materials and total internal reflection. Over the past decades, a broad range of photonic phenomena has demonstrated that electromagnetic energy can also be guided and localized inside low-index regions or nanoscale void cavities. What first appears to be a curiosity is, in fact, highly relevant: The interaction between light and matter lies at the heart of much in optics and photonics. It enables sensing, nonlinear optical phenomena, and optical manipulation, yet it also inevitably introduces absorption, dissipation, and loss. Pushing localized, enhanced, or guided energy into a lower-index space thus offers entirely new possibilities for light-matter interaction and dispersion control. In this review, we discuss some of these counterintuitive structures, starting with light guidance within optically thin media, such as hollow-core photonic crystal fibers or antiresonant reflecting optical waveguides. We then discuss the optics of bubbles, that is, low-index inclusions in a higher-index surrounding, and ultimately arrive at the so-called Mie void resonators, optical resonators that support localized electromagnetic modes confined within a region of lower refractive index. All these systems demonstrate that there are (resonant) optics beyond simple total internal reflection. Absence can itself become a functional photonic degree of freedom, opening opportunities across sensing, quantum nanophotonics, metasurfaces, and programmable optical matter.

title: Plasma morphology under nanosecond repetitively pulsed discharges with air cross-flow: A simulation study
summary: Nanosecond repetitively pulsed discharges in air cross-flows exhibit distinct plasma morphologies that can expand the spatial extent of bulk plasma regions and increase the residence time of reactive radicals within the flow field. This work develops a high-fidelity plasma-fluid simulation framework within OpenFOAM that couples drift-diffusion-convection transport, electrostatic potential, photoionization, mixture-averaged transport, ambipolar diffusion, and a local mean electron energy formulation. Using this framework, we systematically investigate plasma morphologies under air cross-flow velocities of 40 and 100 m/s at a repetition frequency of 50 kHz. The simulations show that lower cross-flow velocities promote plasma retention within previously formed channels, resulting in substantial thermal accumulation. In contrast, at higher cross-flow velocities, plasma is rapidly convected downstream, reducing retention between pulses and weakening thermal accumulation. The simulations further reveal the mechanisms responsible for snap-back, in which a subsequent discharge shifts from a previously formed channel to a shorter and more direct path between the electrodes as the conductivity of the previous channel decreases. As a strong electric field develops between the electrodes, electrons are accelerated and intense Joule heating occurs near the anode tip. This process increases the local electron energy, enhances electron production, and generates a stronger discharge current. As the conductivity of the previous channel decreases, the discharge consequently establishes a new path of least resistance directly between the electrodes.

title: Revealing and Mitigating Transmittance and Reflectance Errors in Integrating-Sphere Characterization of High-Albedo Scattering Media
summary: Accurate optical characterization of high-albedo scattering media is fundamentally limited by integrating-sphere measurement errors. Scattering events spatially redistribute photons, leading to lateral beam spread and angular divergence that bias measured reflectance and transmittance. Here, we investigate these deviations, which are quantified and interpreted by using the point spread function (PSF), guided by the radiative transfer equation. Experiments and Monte Carlo modelling show that the widely used external-mount integrating-sphere configuration introduces systematic, configuration-dependent errors that become pronounced when scattering-induced lateral spreading is substantial. Using a normalised PSF to quantify photon redistribution, we map the characteristic lateral spreading length across a broad $(\taus,g)$ parameter space in the high-albedo limit, providing a basis for evaluating errors in specific measurement geometries. We further quantify the influence of measurement geometry and show that, in the pencil-beam limit, maintaining $L/D_{\mathrm{port}}\lesssim 0.01$ reduces the discrepancy arising from the finite collection aperture to approximately \qty{1}{\percent}. In addition, we introduce an internal-mount integrating-sphere protocol that suppresses scattering-related losses and yields transmittance and reflectance measurements in good agreement with theoretical predictions. Overall, our work helps users of integrating-sphere measurements identify scattering-related errors and improve the reliability of transmittance and reflectance characterization across a wide range of application areas.

title: Cross-coupled photon avalanche drives room-temperature intrinsic optical bistability
summary: Optically bistable materials promise technological advances in optical information processing, memristive devices, and multiparametric sensing. However, optical bistability is predominantly observed under cryogenic conditions or is governed by subtle thermo-optical nonlinearities. Here, we report on Ho3+-activated nanocrystals that exhibit cavity-free intrinsic optical bistability (IOB) at ambient conditions. Non-thermal IOB stems from a cross-coupled photon avalanche (XPA) mechanism enabled by a low-phonon-energy double-perovskite host, which reduces nonradiative losses and facilitates excited-state population via XPA, even when the pump intensity is below threshold. Time-resolved luminescence measurements support the proposed XPA, as evidenced by a double-rise profile consistent with two reservoir states interlocked in energy looping. IOB with high-contrast photoswitching (up to 46 dB) is observed at room temperature across multiple visible emission lines, enabling wavelength-division multiplexing and compatibility with common detectors. IOB is preserved across nano- to microscale crystals and different double-perovskite compositions, broadly enabling information photonics and advanced sensing.

title: RADICAL: Reconfiguration-Aware Direct-Connect AI Cluster using Spatial-and-Wavelength Selective Switching
comment: 14 pages, 16 figures, Accepted for publication in the Journal of Optical Communications and Networking (JOCN), Oct. 2026
summary: We present RADICAL, the silicon-photonic-enabled Reconfiguration-Aware Direct-Connect AI Cluster that integrates a custom spatial-and-wavelength selective switch (SWSS) with the Linux network stack. RADICAL deploys a packaged 4x4x4$λ$ microring-based SWSS into a four-GPU-server cluster using standard SFP28 optical transceivers, and a reconfiguration-aware host-networking interface to demonstrate a direct-connect reconfigurable optical fabric. The SWSS provides dynamic spatial and wavelength routing with 3.2-6.8 dB path loss, average wavelength and spatial crosstalk isolation exceeding 25 dB, and error-free 25 Gbps signal recovery across routing paths. At the system level, RADICAL validates reconfiguration-aware operation through continuous bulk data transfers totaling 6.4 TBytes over 10 minutes. We further demonstrate multitenant AI training across reconfigurable link topologies, including four ResNet-18 instances and six nanoGPT instances, with the latter sustained for more than five hours.

title: Multiport photonic routing with a single cavity-based electro-optic phase shifter per port
comment: 56 pages, including 41 pages of Supplementary Information; 32 figures (4 main-text and 28 supplementary)
summary: Programmable photonic meshes can perform general linear transformations, but universal transformations on $N$ modes require $O(N^2)$ programmable phase shifters, which cannot simultaneously achieve low drive voltage, gigahertz speed, zero static power, lossless modulation, and a compact footprint. Signal routing does not require universal transformations, which allows considerable circuit simplifications. We present a compact reflective circuit architecture that connects all input-output pairs across $N$ modes in $N$ steps using only $O(N)$ programmable phase shifters. The circuit comprises a single passive $N\times N$ interferometer and a single column of programmable reflective phase shifters. We demonstrate the architecture by implementing a $3\times 3$ router in x-cut thin-film lithium niobate with a passive multimode interferometer and phase shifters based on single-sided photonic-crystal nanobeam cavities. Our programmable devices exhibit a $1.92$ GHz/V resonance tuning efficiency via the Pockels effect, a footprint of $100\,μ\mathrm{m}^2$, sub-5-V drive voltage, and a 6.2 GHz electro-optic bandwidth. Through voltage-space characterization and physical modeling, we identify routing states with extinction ratios exceeding 11 dB at each output and demonstrate sequential routing at an equipment-limited speed of 10 MHz. Our results establish cavity-enhanced Pockels switching as a routing layer for classical and quantum computing interconnects across visible and near-infrared wavelengths.

title: Generating entanglement in quantum matter with pathway-entangled photons via resonant inelastic X-ray scattering
summary: Resonant inelastic X-ray scattering (RIXS) is conventionally used to probe elementary excitations and correlations in quantum materials. Here, we propose an interferometric RIXS protocol that instead creates entanglement between spatially separated regions of a solid-state material. An incident X-ray photon is coherently split by a beam splitter into two arms illuminating opposite ends of a sample. Recombining the scattered photons at a second beam splitter and detecting an energy-selected photon then projects the material into a coherent superposition of excitations at the two ends. This protocol is the X-ray, solid-state analogue of the Duan-Lukin-Cirac-Zoller (DLCZ) heralding scheme. Using a Kramers-Heisenberg formalism with quantized photon modes, we show that orthogonal and degenerate end excitations yield maximally entangled states. We illustrate this mechanism in three models: (1) two decoupled sites yield a heralded Bell state. (2) An open tight-binding chain exhibits reflection-parity-dependent interference, providing a benchmark for the interferometer's coherence. (3) A spin-1 Haldane (AKLT) chain yields an entangled pair of fractionalized edge spins. We also discuss practical considerations and challenges for realizing the protocol in X-ray experiments.

title: Nonclassicality from Incomplete Fock-State Statistics
comment: Main text: 7 pages, 5 figures; Supplemental Material: 22 pages, 12 figures
summary: Nonclassicality in bosonic systems can be certified directly from occupation probabilities without full state reconstruction. To complete a library of such criteria we introduce a numerical framework that constructs optimal linear nonclassicality witnesses from arbitrary subsets of measured occupation probabilities by solving a semi-infinite linear program. The method contains known analytical criteria as special cases while generally detecting substantially larger nonclassical regions. We provide an open-source implementation of the numerical optimization together with the analytical criteria discussed here, enabling direct application of the framework to measured occupation statistics across bosonic platforms. As a case study, we apply it to the resonant Jaynes--Cummings model with thermal states and reveal nonclassicality at short interaction times and close to thermal balance, where detection of nonclassicality is otherwise challenging.

title: Electron Wavefronts Capture Nanoscale Movies of Hypersound at Surfaces
comment: 22 pages including 5 pages of Supplementary Information, 5 main figures, 2 Extended Data figures, 8 supplementary videos
summary: Acoustic waves transport mechanical energy and elastic strain through solids, with material composition and shape governing their propagation. In the gigahertz hypersound regime, acoustic wavelengths reach tens to hundreds of nanometres, comparable to nanoscale device dimensions. Harnessing these waves underpins high-frequency signal processing, sensing, electromagnetic coupling and quantum control. Acoustic metrology probes elastic modes and internal interfaces. Yet directly imaging how nanoscale acoustic waves interact with local structure remains challenging, requiring picometre displacement sensitivity combined with high spatiotemporal resolution. Here we demonstrate full-field imaging of laser-induced hypersound at surfaces using reflected electron wavefronts. We introduce ultrafast low-energy electron microscopy (ULEEM), exploiting the intrinsic surface sensitivity of few-electronvolt electrons. Coherent electron pulses down to femtosecond durations reflect from the topmost atomic layers, imprinting the evolving surface profile onto their wavefronts. Defocus converts phase variations into image contrast. In a thin van der Waals material, we image the thermoelastic generation and propagation of picometre-amplitude acoustic waves. Measured dispersion relations, interpreted through elastodynamic modelling, distinguish substrate-supported and locally detached regions, revealing how interfacial contact shapes propagation. Delayed wave emission reveals scattering at buried mechanical defects. Our results establish electron-wavefront imaging of nanoscale surface dynamics, enabling the exploration of ultrafast energy transport, structural transformations and coupled mechanical, electronic and magnetic phenomena.

title: High Resolution Hyperspectral Quantum Infrared Imaging with Undetected Photons
summary: Quantum sensing in the infrared regime often demands the use of expensive and cryogenically operated detectors. Nonlinear interferometry has paved the way for information transfer from the infrared to the near--infrared or visible regime in various quantum technologies. A particularly interesting application of these interferometers involves spectrally--resolved quantum imaging using undetected photons, enabled by the use of temperature--tunable parametric amplifiers. In this work, we demonstrate spectrally resolved transmission imaging with undetected photons around 1550 nm using a spontaneous parametric down conversion based folded nonlinear interferometric scheme, registering the attenuation of a zebrafish larva as a biological feasibility test. We characterize and calibrate the interferometer, having achieved spectrally resolved interference fringes with a maximum baseline visibility of $\sim 74\%$ in the near--infrared regime. Phase--stepped readout of a grating spectrometer gives a resolving power of $\sim1460$ (from the spectrometer's point spread function) at 1550 nm, and $\sim 730$ from the coherence length, the finest reported for imaging with undetected photons, over an instantaneous spectral window of $\approx 51$ cm$^{-1}$.

title: Bogoliubov Dynamics and Zitterbewegung in Optical Dirac Systems
summary: We develop a bosonic Bogoliubov description of Zitterbewegung in time-dependent optical-Dirac systems. Within the optical-Dirac framework, the anomalous pair-creation and pair-annihilation terms of a bosonic Bogoliubov Hamiltonian correspond to couplings between the positive- and negative-frequency sectors, whose coherence underlies the Zitterbewegung response. When the constitutive parameters vary in time, the resulting moving-frame connection generates dynamical interbranch coupling and positive--negative-frequency coherence. Under periodic modulation, this coupling becomes resonant near $Ω\simeq2ω_0$, leading to parametric amplification of the coherence and consequently to an enhanced Zitterbewegung motion.

title: Robustness of Quantum Correlations and Controlled Teleportation Fidelity under Noisy Channels
summary: In distributed quantum computing, quantum networks provide a potential infrastructure for long-range quantum information processing. Controlled quantum teleportation (CQT) is a key practically relevant protocol that can connect two parties on a network and enables a third party, the controller to allow or abort the secure teleportation of an arbitrary single-qubit state between the two parties. We investigate the robustness of a three-qubit GHZ resource under bit-flip, phase-flip, depolarizing, and amplitude-damping noise. Using the Kraus-operator formalism, we characterize the noisy resource through multipartite quantum discord, genuine multipartite concurrence (GMC), localizable entanglement (LE), and CQT fidelity. We also outline a proof-of-concept photonic implementation for preparing the three-qubit GHZ resource and realizing the CQT protocol, which could enable experimental investigation of the effects of noise. Our results show that bit-flip and amplitude-damping noise generally preserve useful mutipartite quantum correlations over broader noise parameter ranges. Interestingly, multipartite discord exhibits freezing under bit-flip noise over a finite parameter regime. Moreover, discord can persist beyond the sudden death of genuine multipartite entanglement, revealing the distinct robustness of nonclassical correlations. We further demonstrate that CQT fidelity which characterizes the performance of CQT can exceed the classical threshold even after GMC vanishes, while LE more closely reflects the operational usefulness of the noisy resource. These findings highlight the complementary roles of quantum correlations and entanglement in assessing the resilience of GHZ-based protocols.

title: Sub-monolayer tracking of molecular states at buried interfaces
summary: Phenomena responsible for emerging technologies originate from novel molecular states at buried interfaces. Yet quantitatively resolving these features is out of reach in most cases. Resonant scattering has demonstrated sensitivity to these local states but is limited due to a lack of accurate interpretive models. We leverage a machine learning (ML)-optimized optical model to analyze polarized resonant soft X-ray scattering (RSoXS) from molecular thin films. This new analysis establishes the direct and quantitative interpretation of molecular orientation, chemical identity and packing states as a function of depth with sub-monolayer resolution - reaching beyond the diffraction limit via locking energy and polarization through the optical model. From our analysis, we discover a gradient evolution of molecular orientation and packing emerging from the interface, indicative of competing surface versus bulk growth dynamics and contradicting hypotheses of substrate patterning. This nondestructive insight into buried interfacial formation and final state opens possibilities in controlling interfacial states and phenomena in next-generation technologies.
